doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Parents, the Ph.D. and riding the horse to Los Angeles
summary: Parents saw music as no career; he earned the Ph.D. to please his father, got no teaching jobs, and went to L.A. to enter the record business.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You have some gems in there. I’m wondering going back, were your parents happy with your career choice and were you, are you pleased that you son has gone into music?

Well I was told growing up not to think of music as a career path. It was — my parents were happy that I play piano I guess, you know they didn’t pay any attention to us back then. That’s the bottom line. I mean kids were really free range 60, 70 years ago. But they were happy I play piano I guess, they were proud of me but it was never thought of as something serious to do. My father died when I was 24 years old I guess, 25. So he never saw what the career path turned into. My mother was thrilled that I became known, that people would know her son’s name. That was really thrilling to her. But you know I think the reason that I went and got a Ph.D. was because I was really trying to please my father who obviously sent me the message that music was fine, music was fun, but life was serious. And I had, you know when I passed the oral exam and, you know there’s this moment where somebody says, “Congratulations Doctor Sidran” my feeling was one of great letdown. I felt that’s it? I thought something would change. I thought there would be some bigger payoff to all that work. That’s it, huh? But the real story of why we’re sitting here talking today is it had nothing to do with my intention. It had everything to do with riding the horse in the direction it’s going. Because when I got my Ph.D. I sent out thirty letters of application to different schools around the country to get a teaching job. I still thought, even after playing with The Rolling Stones and Eric Clapton, even after writing songs — I still thought I was going to be a teacher. musician, right? Why me? I mean how can I be a piano player when McCoy Tyner is a piano player? How can I be a songwriter when Jon Hendricks is a songwriter? You know? I just didn’t think there was a way to get there. And I got nothing back. There was no future for me in academics at that time. So I literally said well okay, I’m going to L.A. and I’m going to get in the record business. And that’s what happened. I rode the horse in the direction it was going, and now we’re here talking.
I’m glad you got on that horse.

Oh me too, oh me too. I can’t tell you. I can’t tell you. What a lucky thing. And I remember also you know when I was writing my dissertation and you know I was, there was information all around and I was trying to, you know, synthesize — I was trying to bring this information and try to figure out what I wanted to say and all that sort of thing. And one of the things that I definitely said to myself when I graduated was I don’t want to study the information anymore. I want to become the information. I want to be the information. I want to know what it feels like to get paid at the end of a night, sitting there waiting for the club owner. I want to know — now I was naïve, because not all of what you learn is a lot of fun. But I did get to do that. I did get to learn what it felt like to be a musician and I guess really in the end that was my heart’s deepest desire.
